sentences: On a long, narrow sheet of paper sit two large masses of rock.
Almost everything else is empty.
But in the blank space beneath the rocks float a few very small fish, and at that moment the white paper turns into water.
This is Fish and Rocks, painted in 1699 by the Chinese artist Bada Shanren in the early Qing dynasty.
It is a hanging scroll in ink on paper, the painting itself about one hundred and thirty-five centimetres tall.
Bada Shanren's real name was Zhu Da.
He was born in 1626 into a branch of the Ming imperial family.
When the Manchus conquered China in 1644, he hid his identity by taking refuge in a Buddhist temple and becoming a monk.
Around 1680 he gave up life as a monk and began to support himself by painting and calligraphy.
From 1684 he used the name Bada Shanren.
He remained loyal to the fallen Ming all his life, and his paintings are often read as a quiet form of protest.
Now look at the rocks.
Dark and pale ink spread into each other to build heavy, solid masses.
Yet their shapes lean at odd angles, and you cannot tell what they stand on or where they are rooted.
Then look at the fish.
There are seven of them.
Six are shown from the side, in profile, but one is seen as if from directly above.
For a moment you lose your footing, unsure where you are standing to look at them.
There is no horizon and no shoreline.
With no line between land and water, we cannot say whether the rocks are floating or sunk beneath the surface.
This uncertainty is what makes the picture feel so strange and unsettled.
The artist composed the picture almost like a piece of calligraphy.
He sets large against small, filled against empty, heavy against light.
Beside the huge rocks, the tiny fish look all the smaller, and all the more alone.
Look at the upper right.
There are two short columns of writing, including his signature, Bada Shanren, and several red seals.
He painted this six years before his death, when he was already past seventy.
The scroll came to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York as a bequest from the collector John M.
Crawford Jr. It is a fine example of the bold, enigmatic images Bada Shanren made in the last twenty years of his life.
Step back and see it whole.
Seven small fish swim quietly through a wide, empty space.
Today, try leaving a little empty time in your day, and simply watch what comes to swim in it.
